response: {"text":"The enzyme that breaks down a common antibiotic, produced outside the cells of a certain soil bacterium, showed an unexpected resistance to heat. When the preparation was heated to 70 °C it lost all activity, but after a 30‑minute exposure to 100 °C a substantial fraction of activity remained. This remaining activity stayed unchanged even after additional heating between 40 °C and 100 °C for up to an hour. The heat‑treated enzyme kept the same optimal pH (around neutral) and temperature (about body temperature) as the untreated sample, and both forms bound the antibiotic substrate with equal efficiency, indicating similar catalytic behavior. The results imply that heating at 100 °C causes the protein to form a stable complex that resists further denaturation. Adding specific metal ions before heating enhanced this stability, likely by promoting complex formation, whereas a plant‑derived polysaccharide reduced stability, probably by blocking protein aggregation. A commonly used protein stabilizer appeared to aid complex formation, further protecting the enzyme from heat."}
